title: Decision Helper: Compare Your Options
problem: New users often ask AI 'what should I do?' and get a wishy-washy non-answer, because the model doesn't know what actually matters to them — it needs your criteria, not just your options, to give a useful recommendation.

workflow.detail: Name the 2–5 choices you're deciding between. More than that tends to make any comparison muddy and less useful.
In your own words, ideally ranked — cost, time, risk, convenience, whatever it actually is for this decision. This is the part a generic pros/cons list is missing.
Run the Prompt Template to get the options compared specifically against your stated criteria, not a generic feature list.
Ask which option the model would pick given your criteria, and why. A forced pick with reasoning is more useful than 'it depends.'

workflow.step: 5. Treat it as one input, not the decision
workflow.detail: Especially for anything high-stakes — money, health, relationships, legal matters — use this as a way to organize your own thinking, then decide yourself or consult a qualified professional.

variables.name: OPTIONS
variables.label: Your options
variables.placeholder: e.g. Option A: used car, $8k, 60k miles. Option B: new car lease, $280/month.

variables.name: CRITERIA
variables.label: What matters to you (ranked)
variables.placeholder:
1. Lowest total cost over 3 years
2. Low chance of surprise repair bills
3. Don't want a long-term commitment

exampleOutput:
| Criterion | Used Car | New Lease |
|---|---|---|
| 3-year total cost | ~$9,500 incl. est. repairs | ~$10,080, no repair risk |
| Repair risk | Moderate — older vehicle | Low — under warranty |
| Commitment | None after purchase | 3-year lease term |

**Recommendation:** Given your #1 priority is lowest total cost and #3 is avoiding long-term commitment, the used car edges out — the lease's predictability comes at the cost of the multi-year commitment you said you want to avoid.
tips: Keep to 2–5 options — beyond that, the comparison gets muddy and harder to act on.
State criteria in your own words and rough order of importance — this is what turns a generic pros-and-cons list into an actual recommendation.
For high-stakes decisions (financial, medical, legal), treat the output as one input among several, not the final word — say so explicitly and consult a qualified professional.
If the recommendation surprises you, ask why — the reasoning is often more useful than the pick itself.
